passage: I'm Shalini, and on Thursday I sat through a film society meeting that ran ninety minutes without a single agenda item. Yusuf spoke first, and he kept going: posters, a guest speaker, the hall booking, then posters again. Two juniors opened their mouths and closed them. Nobody took notes. When it ended, people simply stood up. In the corridor one person said the guest talk was cancelled, another said postponed, and someone else thought they'd been asked to book the hall. I had written "budget?" in my notebook and never got to ask it. Later I heard Yusuf tell someone the meeting had been really productive. I'm not sure he noticed how many of us left with different answers.

qa.q: How long did the film society meeting run?
qa.a: It ran ninety minutes without a single agenda item.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when Shalini wrote "budget?" in the notebook and never got to ask it?
qa.a: Frustrated and unheard, since the question never had a place in the meeting.

qa.q: What could the group do next time so everyone leaves with the same outcome?
qa.a: Send a short agenda beforehand, give each item a few minutes and write down the decisions before people leave.

qa.q: Why might Yusuf see the meeting differently from the others?
qa.a: Yusuf probably felt it was productive because he got to talk through many ideas, and did not notice people left with different memories.

grounding: Shows a participant watching a meeting with no agenda where one voice dominates and everyone leaves with a different outcome.

passage:
Monday. Rukmini, an intern, sat in a one-hour team meeting with no agenda. Payal, the loudest voice in the room, talked about the client, the website and the holiday rota, jumping between them, and the meeting ended when the lunch trolley arrived. Nobody said what had been decided.

Wednesday. Two team members had each started the same slide deck, and nobody had begun the client email. Rukmini had written "deck?" in her notebook on Monday and now saw why.

Friday. Payal asked, "Who is doing the email?" Three people gave three different answers about who had agreed to it. An hour was lost sorting it out, and Rukmini decided to keep a list of decisions and share it after every meeting.

qa.q: What ended the Monday meeting?
qa.a: The lunch trolley arriving ended the meeting.

qa.q: What was Rukmini thinking on Wednesday when she saw the two slide decks?
qa.a: Rukmini understood why she had written "deck?" in her notebook, and probably felt frustrated at the wasted effort.

qa.q: What could Rukmini do after Friday's confusion?
qa.a: Keep a list of decisions and share it after each meeting so everyone has the same record.

qa.q: How might Payal have experienced the Monday meeting compared with the others?
qa.a: Payal probably felt it went smoothly because Payal did most of the talking, and did not notice that others left unsure of what was decided.

grounding: Shows an attendee living with the results of a meeting with no agenda, no record of decisions and different memories.

passage:
Rashmi, you are going to your first club meeting tomorrow? Then listen to your Kalyani maasi for five minutes.
In my second year of college, I joined the fest committee. The first meeting was in the canteen, at four. No list, no topic. The general secretary, Bhushan, talked for most of the hour about a band he wanted. Two girls tried to raise the budget. He laughed and went on. I sat at the end of the bench and said nothing. I kept waiting for someone to write something down. Nobody did.
We got up at five-thirty. On the way out, one friend said we had chosen the band. Another said we had chosen a play. I thought we had decided nothing.
Two weeks later, two groups had booked the same hall for the same day. Bhushan shouted at everyone. I remember thinking, if only one person had asked, "So what did we decide?"

qa.q: Where was the first meeting held?
qa.a: The first meeting was in the canteen, at four.

qa.q: What was young Kalyani feeling as she sat at the end of the bench?
qa.a: Kalyani felt uneasy and frustrated, waiting for someone to write something down while one voice took over the hour.

qa.q: At what point in the story could one question have changed the result?
qa.a: At the end of the meeting, if someone had asked what was decided and written it down, the double booking might not have happened.

qa.q: How might Bhushan have felt when the two groups booked the same hall?
qa.a: Bhushan was probably angry and embarrassed, which is why he shouted at everyone instead of seeing that his meeting had decided nothing.

grounding: An elder recalls sitting through a meeting with no agenda where the loudest voice dominated and everyone remembered a different decision.

passage:
The team met in a café because the office internet was down, and the coffee machine hissed every two minutes. Vijay, an intern for three weeks, had his notebook open and a pen ready.
There was no agenda. Mehak, the product manager, started on the new app screen, then slid into a story about a client, then into the new logo. Arun from sales cut in loudly and argued about pricing for twenty minutes. Every time Vijay leaned forward to ask a question, the machine hissed or Arun's voice rose.
After ninety minutes Mehak said, "Great, so we're aligned," and stood up.
On the walk back, Vijay asked the designer what they had aligned on. "The new colours," she said. Arun, on the phone, was telling someone that pricing was settled. Vijay looked at his notebook. Two pages of arrows and not a single line he could call a decision. He had a report due at five.

qa.q: Why did the team meet in a café?
qa.a: The team met in a café because the office internet was down.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling as he looked at his notebook on the walk back?
qa.a: Vijay felt confused and anxious, with two pages of arrows, no decision to report and a report due at five.

qa.q: What could have made this meeting useful?
qa.a: A short agenda, someone keeping Arun's pricing argument to time, and ending with the decisions read aloud would have left everyone with the same outcome.

qa.q: How does Mehak see the meeting?
qa.a: Mehak seems to think it went well, saying "we're aligned," without noticing that people left with different memories.

grounding: Shows an intern watching a meeting with no agenda, dominated by the loudest voice, that ends with each person remembering a different outcome.

passage:
The housing society's youth committee met in the clubhouse in Andheri on Sunday morning to plan the Diwali evening. Chandrika, in her final year of college, sat near the door with her tea.
Shalini, the committee secretary, spoke first and kept speaking: last year's lights, a caterer she liked, the parking problem, a neighbour's dog. Two younger boys tried to suggest a quiz. Shalini said, "Nice, nice," and carried on. Nobody had a list. Chandrika checked her watch twice. An hour and a half passed.
When they broke up, Chandrika's phone buzzed with the group chat. "So we're doing the caterer, right?" "I thought we agreed on potluck?" "Is the quiz happening or not?" Four messages, four versions.
Chandrika scrolled, then put the phone face down. She had given up a morning of study for this, and she could not tell her mother a single thing they had decided.

qa.q: What did the two younger boys try to suggest?
qa.a: They tried to suggest a quiz.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel when she put the phone face down?
qa.a: Chandrika felt frustrated and let down, having given up a morning of study for a meeting where nothing was decided.

qa.q: What small change could the committee try next time?
qa.a: Someone could write a short list of items before the meeting, give each a time limit and read out the decisions at the end.

qa.q: How might Shalini see the same morning?
qa.a: Shalini may think the meeting went well because she covered many points, without noticing others could not get a word in.

grounding: Illustrates a participant watching a meeting with no agenda, where one voice dominates and the group leaves with four different versions of the plan.

passage:
"So, the mess menu," Rajat said, before anyone else could speak. "Paneer three times a week. Obviously."
"Is there a list of what we're—" Sumit began.
"And the Sunday special should be biryani. I've said this for a year."
"What about late dinner for the lab students?" Ganga asked.
"Later, later. First, paneer."
Forty minutes passed. Rajat talked about paneer, the cook's attitude, a cricket match, paneer again. Sumit watched the clock and the three first-years at the back who hadn't said a word.
"Okay, good meeting," Rajat said, standing. "Done."
Outside, Sumit asked, "So what did we decide?"
"Late dinner moves to nine thirty," Ganga said.
"Did it? I thought he said later."
"I heard 'fine, later'."
"And paneer?"
"Three times. Or twice. Honestly, not sure."
Sumit rubbed his eyes. "An hour gone, and we each walked out of a different meeting."

qa.q: How long did Rajat keep talking before the meeting ended?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel walking out of the meeting?
qa.a: Sumit was frustrated and confused, rubbing his eyes because an hour had gone and nobody knew what had been decided.

qa.q: What could have made the meeting useful?
qa.a: A short agenda read out at the start, a turn for each item, and someone repeating each decision at the end so everyone left with the same outcome.

qa.q: What is it like for Ganga when the late-dinner question is brushed aside?
qa.a: Ganga is pushed aside by the loudest voice and then leaves unsure whether the question was even answered, which feels dismissive and wasteful.

grounding: Shows a participant sitting through a meeting with no agenda where the loudest voice dominates and everyone leaves remembering a different outcome.
